title: Our duty to praise
hook: once a High Holy Day prayer, now said at the end of every service

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mi Sheberach: the blessing for the sick, the community and the country. Your line was pray for the city. Whose name did you hold up? Today, the prayer that closes almost every service. Day six hundred two.

Morning, afternoon or evening, the last few minutes of a synagogue service tend to sound alike. People stand. The tune picks up. And at one line, the room bends its knees and bows, together. It sounds like an ending that was always there. Historians say otherwise. For a long stretch, this prayer belonged to Rosh Hashanah, the New Year, in the solemn season of the High Holy Days. Then, sometime in the Middle Ages, it moved. Out of the High Holy Days, and into every single day.
screen: `THE WHOLE ROOM BOWS.` → `ONCE A NEW YEAR PRAYER.` → `NOW EVERY DAY.`

segments.voice: Its first word is aleinu: it is upon us. It is our duty. The opening says, roughly, it is our duty to praise the Master of all, to give greatness to the one who formed the world. Then comes the bowing line: and we bend the knee and bow and give thanks before the King of kings. That's when people bow. Where did it come from? Tradition credits Joshua. Some scholars connect it with the sage Rav in Babylonia, who is said to have arranged the Rosh Hashanah prayers about God's kingship, and Aleinu opens that section. On the High Holy Days it still keeps its old drama: in many synagogues the cantor, and sometimes everyone, kneels and lowers all the way to the floor, a posture the rest of the year's prayers don't ask for. The second paragraph turns outward, toward a hope. It looks to a day when the world will be repaired under the kingship of God. The Hebrew phrase there, l'taken olam, to repair the world, is one of the roots of the modern words tikkun olam. And it ends with a verse from Zechariah, in the old Jewish translation: "And the LORD shall be King over all the earth; in that day shall the LORD be One, and His name one." So the prayer moves in two steps. First, our duty to praise, right now, on our knees. Then the hope that one day the whole world will join in. The service ends holding both.
screen: `ALEINU: IT IS UPON US.` · `WE BEND THE KNEE AND BOW.` · `FROM ROSH HASHANAH TO EVERY DAY.` · `TO REPAIR THE WORLD.` · then, large: `OUR DUTY TO PRAISE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bow at we bend the knee. Stand, if you can, and settle your breath. If you pray, you can say the opening line in your own language: it is our duty to praise. When you reach we bend the knee and bow, do just that. Bend your knees a little. Bow from the waist. Come back up slowly. Then stay standing and breathe, and let your body remember what it just said. The bell holds the time.
Aleinu. It is upon us. The prayer of duty and hope that closes the service, with a bow in the middle.

Your line: our duty to praise. A week of Tachanun, the ark opening, the yad, lifting the scroll, the haftarah, Mi Sheberach and Aleinu. Today, praise one thing out loud that you'd usually pass by. Day six hundred two.

howItsDone: Aleinu is said standing at the end of the morning, afternoon and evening services, and many people bend the knees and bow at the line about bending the knee; on the High Holy Days many congregations kneel and prostrate fully during it.

fork.setup: you're standing at the end of the service, saying Aleinu. you reach the words we bend the knee and bow. what does the room do?
fork.reveal: people bend their knees and bow at those very words; on the High Holy Days some go all the way to the floor.

trapdoor: what you thought: a closing song so everyone knows the service is ending.
what it means: a statement of duty, to praise now, and a hope that the whole world will one day be repaired.
what a scholar hears: an opening to the Rosh Hashanah kingship verses, linked with Rav, that moved into daily prayer in medieval Europe.

notes: Zechariah 14:9 quoted from JPS 1917 from memory; verify.
Attribution: tradition credits Joshua; many scholars link it to Rav (3rd century) and the Rosh Hashanah Malchuyot. Confirm wording.
Aleinu entered the daily service in medieval Ashkenaz (often dated to the 12th–14th centuries); left vague as 'sometime in the Middle Ages'.
Full prostration on the High Holy Days: practice varies (cantor only in some congregations, everyone in others).
The bowing line echoes Isaiah 45:23; paraphrased, not quoted.
The medieval censorship of a line of Aleinu is deliberately omitted.
Week-end look-back (days 596–602) placed in the carry.

Editor review (y2 595–612): hook no longer opens 'Walk into almost any' or tells the listener how it feels; 'the most solemn part of the year' superlative cut; the history now attributed to historians. 'Many scholars' and 'third-century' cut (claims rule) to 'some scholars' and 'is said to have arranged'; 'one of the only times in the Jewish year' (unsourced; Yom Kippur's Avodah also has prostration) replaced in teach and myth; 'you walk out with both in your pocket' changed so it doesn't speak for the listener.
